(High confidence) We assess the Hithium-Lightsource relationship as real, single-deal, and geographically fenced: one 640 MWh Australian contract plus a prospectus naming — with no US or UK extension possible under current rules (the US book is FEOC-clean by design: ~8.3 GW of First Solar modules, all-domestic marketing, ITC-dependent financing) and no Australian incumbency lock (Lower Wonga went to Gotion).

(High confidence) We assess ownership volatility as the dominant account risk: bp is mid-process on selling the entire platform (Wren House/Qualitas reported), the UK O&M arm is separately for sale, and the Woolooga asset itself may now belong to Aula Energy — meaning the counterparty that signed Hithium's contract, the entity that owns the asset at COD, and the owner who decides future procurement may be three different organizations within a year.

(Moderate confidence) We assess the practical Hithium plays as: (1) deliver Woolooga to energization flawlessly — it is the Australian reference asset and the prospectus proof point; (2) chase the retained 9.5 GW+ APAC hybrid pipeline (explicitly aimed at data-center/AI demand) where Chinese supply competes freely and INTEC relationships carry over; (3) track the Aula BESS options (~800 MWh) — the buyer of those options inherits the procurement decision; (4) treat the US storage whitespace (Big Bronco/Zion Valley/Golden Plains, suppliers unnamed) as unwinnable for ITC-claiming vintages absent a FEOC-compliant structure.

(High confidence) For the Hithium lens: Lightsource proves the export-market playbook works — win where FEOC doesn't reach, on price-competitive 5 MWh hardware with long warranties and a local O&M partner — and simultaneously proves its ceiling: no co-marketing gravity, no framework, contestable follow-ons, and a customer whose US half is structurally closed.

Huawei was already excluded by the Entity List and NDAA 889, so its incremental loss is minimal; Sungrow, which retains US market access, absorbed the shock instead, shedding roughly CNY 100B (~$14.8B) of market value over the following month.

Two limits on scope are load-bearing and should be tracked rather than assumed: the prohibition is prospective only, leaving pre-28-July authorizations saleable, and the definition requires BOTH bi-directional DC-AC conversion AND remote connectivity via "Wi-Fi, cellular, Bluetooth or another similar connection" — Sungrow has publicly argued its products fall outside on the second prong because it restricts connection activity to wired links.

FCC adds foreign-produced connected power inverters to the Covered List, blocking new US equipment authorizations — Supersedes the 30 June draft reporting and lands broader than trailed: the FCC names no company or country — the test is whether a device fails the Buy American "domestic end product" standard (48 CFR 25.101(a)), so it is an origin rule, not a China rule, and catches Taiwanese, Korean and US-brand offshore production alike. We assess the direct incremental effect on Huawei is near zero — the Entity List and NDAA 889 already closed the US — but the competitive effect is material: it closes the US to Sungrow and the rest of the Chinese inverter bloc on the same terms, and opens a US-onshoring race via the Conditional Approval route (Department of War or DHS, applications to 1 January 2028, requiring a time-bound US manufacturing plan). Restriction is prospective only; pre-28-July authorizations survive.

a.note: Recip-capacity rival eroding the time-limited moat.
a.context: VoltaGrid's moat — ≥3.8 GW of locked INNIO Jenbacher production while GE Vernova heavy-duty slots quote into 2031 — is time-limited: recip capacity is scaling industry-wide (Cat, Cummins, Wärtsilä), and interconnection reform would collapse the speed premium that justifies ~$1,700-2,000/kW gas at 55-65% overbuild.

a.note: 14 mobile units (~35 MW) powered the Colossus 122-day bring-up — the pivot's proof point.
a.context: June 2024: 14 VoltaGrid mobile units (~35 MW) powered xAI Colossus's 122-day, 100k-GPU bring-up before grid power and Tesla Megapacks arrived — the deployment that migrated the fleet from frac pads to AI and seeded the AIDC franchise. Bridge-scope, superseded at the site by permanent power.

b.note: Mobile gas fleet (~35 MW) bridged the Colossus 1 bring-up.
b.context: Fourteen VoltaGrid mobile units (~35 MW of Jenbacher-engine generation) powered Colossus 1's 122-day, 100k-GPU bring-up in mid-2024 before grid power (MLGW/TVA) and Tesla Megapacks arrived. Bridge-scope, since superseded — permanent power now runs through the Solaris JV turbines, MLGW substations and Megapack buffering.

evid.text: For the relationship web: it is FEOC-clean by construction (Austrian engines, Swiss electricals, Texas manufacturing), its growth shrinks the addressable BESS layer on the fastest-growing off-grid segment, and where batteries did attach at its sites (xAI Colossus, where VoltaGrid's 35 MW mobile fleet bridged the 122-day bring-up), the buyer precedent was Tesla Megapack.

(Moderate confidence) We assess the residual battery surfaces at VoltaGrid as real but closed to Hithium: the legacy mobile fleet carries undisclosed BESS on its switchgear bus (a small, incumbent-held socket), and bridge-power sites have paired with Tesla Megapacks (xAI precedent) — a §154-named supplier has no visible path into either, and VoltaGrid's FEOC-clean-by-construction stack is part of its customer pitch even if never stated as such.
